title: Assign Cookies
summary: Child i is content with a cookie of size at least g[i]; each child gets at most one cookie. Return the most content children.
statement:
Child `i` is content only with a cookie of size at least `g[i]` (their greed factor). Cookie `j` has size `s[j]`. Each child can get at most one cookie and each cookie can go to at most one child.

Return the maximum number of content children.
hints: Wasting a big cookie on a child who would be happy with a small one can only hurt.
Sort both arrays. Try to satisfy the least greedy child with the smallest cookie that is big enough.
Use two pointers: if the current cookie satisfies the current child, move on to the next child; either way, move to the next cookie.
explain: Both cookies have size 1, so only the child whose greed is 1 can be satisfied. The answer is 1.

title: Best Time to Buy and Sell Stock
summary: Choose one day to buy and a later day to sell. Return the maximum profit, or 0.
statement:
`prices[i]` is the price of a stock on day `i`. Choose one day to buy one share and a later day to sell it.

Return the maximum profit you can make, or `0` if no profitable trade exists.

You must buy before you sell, and you make at most one trade. Track the lowest price seen so far and the best profit from selling today.
hints: If you sell on day i, the best day to buy is the cheapest day before it.
Scan once, tracking the lowest price seen so far.
At each day, the profit of selling today is price − minSoFar. Keep the maximum.
explain: Buy on day 1 at price 1 and sell on day 4 at price 6, a profit of 5. Selling at 7 is impossible because day 0 comes before the buy, so the answer is 5.

title: Jump Game
summary: nums[i] is the furthest jump from index i. Starting at index 0, return whether you can reach the last index.

perf.label: 10,000 positions, end unreachable
perf.gen: int[] a0 = new int[10000]; Arrays.fill(a0, 3); for (int i = 9995; i <= 9998; i++) a0[i] = 0;

statement:
You start at index `0` of `nums`. `nums[i]` is the maximum length of a jump from index `i` (you can jump any shorter distance too).

Return `true` if you can reach the last index.

For example in `[3,2,1,0,4]` every route gets stuck at the 0 at index 3, so the answer there is `false`.
hints: You do not need to choose actual jumps; you only need to know how far you could possibly get.
Track the furthest index reachable so far while scanning from the left.
If you ever stand on an index beyond that furthest reach, you are stuck: return false. Otherwise update reach = max(reach, i + nums[i]).
explain: Jump 1 step from index 0 to index 1, then 3 steps from index 1 to the last index. The end is reachable, so the answer is `true`.

title: Jump Game II
summary: nums[i] is the furthest jump from index i, and the end is always reachable. Return the fewest jumps from index 0 to the last index.
statement:
You start at index `0` of `nums`, and `nums[i]` is the maximum length of a jump from index `i`. The last index is always reachable.

Return the minimum number of jumps needed to reach the last index.

Think of the jumps in waves: everything reachable with one jump, then everything reachable from those, and so on. Count the waves until the last index is covered.
hints: Think in "levels", as in BFS: all indices reachable with one jump, then with two, and so on.
Keep the end of the current level and the furthest index reachable from anywhere inside it.
When you reach the end of the current level, you must jump: count one jump and set the level end to the furthest reach. Stop before the last index.
explain: Jump from index 0 to index 1, then from index 1 (which can jump 3) straight to the last index. That is 2 jumps, the fewest possible.

title: Gas Station
summary: Stations on a circle give gas[i] and the trip to the next costs cost[i]. Return the starting station to complete the loop (unique), or -1.
statement:
There are `n` gas stations on a circular route. Station `i` gives you `gas[i]` units of fuel, and driving from station `i` to the next station costs `cost[i]`. You start with an empty tank at one station.

Return the index of the station from which you can drive around the whole circuit once, or `-1` if it is impossible. If a solution exists, it is unique.
hints: If total gas < total cost, no start can work. Otherwise exactly one start does.
Drive from a candidate start, tracking the tank. If it goes negative at station i, no station between the start and i can be the answer either.
So restart the candidate at i + 1 with an empty tank. One pass, O(n).
explain: Starting at station 3 with an empty tank: +4 −1, +5 −2, +1 −3, +2 −4, +3 −5 leaves 3, 6, 4, 2 and finally 0 gas, never below zero. So the trip works from station 3.

title: Partition Labels
summary: Split s into as many parts as possible so each letter appears in at most one part. Return the part sizes in order.
statement:
Split `s` into as many parts as possible so that each letter appears in at most one part. Joined together in order, the parts must form `s`.

Return the sizes of the parts, in order.

For example in "eccbbbbdec", "e" appears at both ends, so the whole string must be a single part of size 10.
hints: A part that contains some letter must extend at least to that letter's last occurrence.
First record the last index of every letter.
Scan with the current part's end = max(end, last[letter]). When the index reaches end, close the part and start a new one.
explain: The parts "ababcbaca", "defegde" and "hijhklij" each contain every copy of their letters, and no part can be split further. Their sizes are `[9,7,8]`.

title: Boats to Save People
summary: Each boat carries at most two people with total weight ≤ limit. Return the fewest boats to carry everyone.
statement:
`people[i]` is the weight of person `i`. Each boat carries at most two people at the same time, as long as their total weight is at most `limit`.

Return the minimum number of boats needed to carry everyone. Every person can fit in a boat on their own.
hints: The heaviest person needs a boat anyway. Who is the best partner for them?
Sort the weights. Pair the heaviest remaining person with the lightest remaining person if they fit together.
Use two pointers from both ends: the heavy pointer always moves, the light pointer moves only when the pair fits. Count one boat per step.
explain: The two people weigh 1 + 2 = 3, exactly the limit, so they share one boat. The answer is 1.

title: Two City Scheduling
summary: costs[i] = [toA, toB]. Send exactly half of the 2n people to each city at minimum total cost.
statement:
A company is interviewing `2n` people. `costs[i] = [aCost, bCost]` is the cost of flying person `i` to city A or to city B.

Exactly `n` people must go to each city. Return the minimum total cost.

Sort people by how much cheaper city A is than city B (`aCost − bCost`), send the first `n` to A and the rest to B.
hints: Imagine sending everyone to B, then choosing n people to switch to A. What does switching person i change?
Switching person i changes the total by aCost − bCost. You want the n most negative (or least positive) changes.
Sort by aCost − bCost; send the first half to A and the rest to B.
explain: Send the first two people to city A (10 + 30) and the last two to city B (50 + 20). The total is 110, the cheapest split with 2 people per city.

title: Candy
summary: Every child gets at least one candy, and a child with a higher rating than a neighbour gets more candies than that neighbour. Return the fewest candies needed.

perf.label: 20,000 children
perf.gen: int[] a0 = new int[20000]; for (int i = 0; i < a0.length; i++) a0[i] = 20000 - i;

statement:
Children stand in a line, and `ratings[i]` is child `i`'s rating. Give out candies so that:

- every child gets at least one candy,
- a child with a higher rating than a neighbour gets more candies than that neighbour.

Return the minimum total number of candies.
hints: Each child has two constraints: one from the left neighbour and one from the right. Handle them separately.
Left to right: if ratings[i] > ratings[i − 1], give candy[i] = candy[i − 1] + 1, otherwise 1.
Right to left: if ratings[i] > ratings[i + 1], set candy[i] = max(candy[i], candy[i + 1] + 1). Sum the result.
explain: The children can get 2, 1 and 2 candies: each child rated higher than a neighbour gets more than that neighbour. That is 5 candies, the fewest possible.

title: Lemonade Change
summary: Lemonade costs $5. Customers pay in order with a $5, $10 or $20 bill, and you start with no change. Return true if you can give every customer correct change.
statement:
At a lemonade stand each lemonade costs `$5`. Customers queue up and buy one at a time, in the order given by `bills`. Each customer pays with a single `$5`, `$10` or `$20` bill, and you must give them the right change so they pay exactly `$5`.

You start with no change at all. Return `true` if you can give every customer correct change, and `false` otherwise.
hints: Only $5 and $10 bills are ever useful as change. Keep a count of each.
A $10 needs one $5 back. A $20 needs $15 back: either one $10 and one $5, or three $5s.
For a $20, prefer giving the $10 + $5. $5 bills are more flexible (they also pay for $10 customers), so save them when you can.
explain: The first three customers pay $5, so you hold three $5 bills. The $10 customer gets one $5 back, and the $20 customer gets the $10 and a $5. Everyone got change, so the answer is `true`.

title: Merge Triplets to Form Target Triplet
summary: An operation replaces triplet j with the element-wise maximum of triplets i and j. Return true if, after any number of operations, some triplet can equal target.
statement:
`triplets[i] = [a_i, b_i, c_i]` and `target = [x, y, z]`. In one operation you pick two different indices `i` and `j` and replace `triplets[j]` with `[max(a_i, a_j), max(b_i, b_j), max(c_i, c_j)]`.

Return `true` if, after any number of operations (possibly none), `target` can appear as one of the triplets.
constraints: Each triplet and target has three values
hints: Merging only ever increases values. So a triplet with any value larger than the target's at the same position can never be used.
Among the usable triplets, merging all of them gives the largest reachable values without overshooting.
The answer is yes exactly when, for each of the three positions, some usable triplet matches the target there.
explain: [1,8,4] can never be used, because 8 overshoots the target's 7. Merging [2,5,3] with [1,7,5] gives [2,7,5], the target, so the answer is `true`.

title: Valid Parenthesis String
summary: s contains "(", ")" and "*", where each "*" may be treated as "(", ")" or nothing. Return true if some choice makes s a valid parentheses string.
statement:
`s` contains only `"("`, `")"` and `"*"`. Return `true` if `s` is valid. It is valid if:

- every `"("` has a matching `")"` after it, and every `")"` has a matching `"("` before it;
- each `"*"` can be treated as a single `"("`, a single `")"`, or an empty string.

For example "(*))" is also valid: treat the "*" as "(" to get "(())".
hints: Trying all three options for every "*" is 3^k work for k stars. A DP over (index, open count) works in O(n²).
Instead of one open count, track the range of possible open counts: lo (treat every "*" as ")") and hi (treat every "*" as "(").
If hi ever drops below 0, too many ")" have appeared: fail. Never let lo go below 0, since a "*" can always be empty instead. The string is valid if lo is 0 at the end.
explain: "()" is already balanced without any stars, so the answer is `true`.

title: Hand of Straights
summary: Return true if the cards in hand can be split into groups of groupSize consecutive values, using every card exactly once.
statement:
Alice wants to rearrange her cards into groups of exactly `groupSize` cards, where each group consists of `groupSize` **consecutive** values (like 3, 4, 5). `hand[i]` is the value written on the `i`-th card.

Return `true` if she can use every card exactly once in such groups, and `false` otherwise.
hints: If the number of cards is not a multiple of groupSize, the answer is false immediately.
The smallest card left must start a group, because no smaller card exists to come before it.
Count the cards in a sorted map. Repeatedly take the smallest value v and remove one of each of v, v + 1, …, v + groupSize − 1; fail if any is missing.
explain: The cards split into [1,2,3], [2,3,4] and [6,7,8], each three consecutive values, so the answer is `true`.

title: Dota2 Senate
summary: Senators of two parties (R = Radiant, D = Dire) act in order, round after round; each can ban one senator of the other party. When only one party can still vote, it wins. Return "Radiant" or "Dire".
statement:
The Dota2 senate has senators from two parties, Radiant (`"R"`) and Dire (`"D"`); `senate[i]` is the party of the `i`-th senator. Voting goes round by round, and in each round the senators act in order from first to last. A senator who has not been banned can do one of two things:

- **ban** one senator of the other party, who loses all rights in this and every later round;
- **announce victory**, if every senator still able to vote belongs to their own party.

Every senator plays the best strategy for their party. Return `"Radiant"` or `"Dire"`, the party that announces victory.
hints: Greedy: each senator should ban the next opposing senator who would act after them, since that opponent is the most immediate threat.
Simulating round by round and scanning for the next opponent costs O(n²).

Use two queues of positions, one per party. Compare the fronts: the earlier one bans the other and re-enters its queue at position + n (the next round); the later one is removed. The party whose queue empties loses.
explain: The Radiant senator acts first and bans the Dire senator. In the next round only Radiant can vote, so "Radiant" announces victory.

title: Jump Game VII
summary: s is a binary string with s[0] = "0". From index i you may jump to j when minJump <= j − i <= maxJump and s[j] = "0". Return true if you can reach the last index.
statement:
`s` is a binary string, and `s[0]` is `"0"`. You start at index `0`. From index `i` you can jump to index `j` if:

- `i + minJump <= j <= min(i + maxJump, s.length − 1)`, and
- `s[j] == "0"`.

Return `true` if you can reach index `s.length − 1`, and `false` otherwise.
hints: reach[j] is true when s[j] is "0" and some reachable i lies in the window [j − maxJump, j − minJump]. Checking the whole window for every j is O(n · (maxJump − minJump)).
Keep a running count of reachable indices inside that window as it slides: add index j − minJump when it enters, remove j − maxJump − 1 when it leaves.
Alternatively, BFS while remembering the farthest index already scheduled, so each index is examined only once.
explain: From index 0, jump 3 to index 3 (a "0"), then jump 2 to index 5, the last index. The answer is `true`.
